status: candidate / pending_human_review (model reading; not a gate verdict)
dataset_family: Local Madrid MCI cohort, Maestu group (Center for Cognitive and Computational Neuroscience, Universidad Complutense de Madrid); MCI recruited 2010-2014 under projects PSI2009-14415-C03-01 and PSI2012-38375-C03-01 from Hospital Universitario Clinico San Carlos, the Center for Prevention of Cognitive Impairment and the Seniors Center of Chamartin; MEG recorded at the Center for Biomedical Technology (CTB), Madrid. 117 MCI analysed (61 vMCI / 56 nvMCI). New relative to the current supporters, but the same lab, MEG site and senior author as the Madrid (CTB) arm of BioFIND used by round-1 candidate P-488.
method_family: Resting-state source-space MEG relative power spectra (LCMV beamformer, cluster-based permutation). Same method family as current supporter P-584 (MEG alpha power) and round-1 candidate P-488 (resting MEG spectral power/covariance).
what_it_shows: Frontiers in Human Neuroscience 2023 (Torres-Simon et al.). Within an MCI-only sample split by a white-matter-hyperintensity volume cut point (3,448 mm3, the 95th percentile of 346 cognitively intact older adults), vascular MCI (high WMH) showed a widespread theta-power increase (CBPT p = 0.036) and bilateral temporo-parietal beta-power decreases (p = 0.0336 and 0.0401) relative to non-vascular MCI, while ICV-normalised hippocampal volume (ANCOVA for age and WM volume: left p = 0.87, right p = 0.80) and cognition did not differ between the two MCI subgroups. All three MEG clusters correlated with hippocampal volume and with cognition across the whole sample. There are no controls in the MEG analysis and no follow-up, so there is no MCI detection and no conversion outcome.
why: Stated form (Table A1: volumetric atrophy late and insufficient; functional/microstructural/mechanical/metabolic measures detect MCI or predict conversion where volume is preserved): NO. The MEG contrast is between two MCI subgroups defined by WMH volume, which is itself a structural MRI lesion-volume measure. MEG therefore tracks vascular lesion burden, not MCI status: no controls were recorded with MEG, no MCI-vs-control detection is run, and there is no longitudinal outcome. The hippocampal-volume null is a null between two MCI subgroups, not a demonstration that volume is preserved in MCI or late relative to MEG. Narrowed form (round 20: non-volumetric measures carried information about MCI status or progression that hippocampal volume did not): NO. The information the MEG clusters carried is information about the WMH-defined split, i.e. about another volumetric MRI measure, not about MCI or progression. Moreover, the clusters were selected by contrasting those same WMH-defined groups, and the authors' statement that the markers matter 'for early differentiation since both MCI groups did not show statistical differences in cognition nor in hippocampal volumes' concerns differentiating vascular from non-vascular MCI, not detecting MCI. The MEG clusters also correlated with hippocampal volume (theta vs RHV rho = -0.282, p = 0.002), so they are not shown to carry information independent of it. The authors' closing claim that MEG may register vascular dysfunction 'before structural changes and/or cognitive decline are evidenced' is an inference in the conclusions, not a tested result. Caveats noted for the record: hippocampal volumes were numerically lower in vMCI (RHV 0.0022 vs 0.0024 ICV fraction) and the nulls are covariate-adjusted; no AD biomarkers were available (authors' limitation). Independence: under H.1 its method family (resting MEG spectral power) duplicates P-584 and P-488. It also shares senior author Fernando Maestu and the CTB Madrid MEG laboratory (same Elekta Vectorview system) with P-488, whose BioFIND data include 90 MCI patients from 'the Laboratory of Cognitive and Computational Neuroscience at the Centre for Biomedical Technology (CTB), Madrid', 'pooled over a number of different projects'. Whether any of P-543's 2010-2014 MCI participants are also in BioFIND's Madrid arm cannot be determined from the two PDFs; BioFIND's Madrid criteria excluded vascular disorders on MRI, so any overlap would most plausibly be in the nvMCI subgroup. Treat as a possible shared sample and a confirmed shared author/site. P-577 is P-488's registry duplicate stub and inherits the same relation. Not a preprint (peer-reviewed journal article). Symbols transliterated to ASCII in quotes (+/- for the plus-minus sign, << for the much-less-than sign, 'theta'/'beta1'/'beta2' for the Greek-letter cluster names, 'Chamartin' for Chamart-i-acute-n).

quotes.quote: The original 117 patients with MCI were divided into two groups (VMCI vs. nVMCI) using their WMH volumes and the 3,448 mm3 cut point. Sixty-one patients diagnosed with MCI showed WMH volumes above the cut point (hence vMCI group) whereas 56 had WMH volumes below the cut point (nvMCI group).

Patients with vMCI showed significantly higher age (p < 0.001), Total gray matter volume (GM volume; p = 0.014) and WMH volume (p <<0.001). No significant differences between groups arise when cognitive performance and hippocampal volumes were assessed.

Although all the patients included in the sample met the MCI diagnosis criteria (Petersen, 2004), the lack of neuropathological markers of AD (i.e., CSF/PET amyloid or tau markers) potentially increases the heterogeneity of the MCI population

Data were collected between 2010 and 2014 in collaboration with three different clinical centers located in Madrid (Spain): the Neurology Department in "Hospital Universitario Clinico San Carlos," the Center for Prevention of Cognitive Impairment, and the Seniors Center of Chamartin District.
Five minutes of resting-state (closed-opened eyes) were recorded with a Vectorview system (Elekta Neuromag) at the Center for Biomedical Technology (Madrid, Spain).
